transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-11
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya (AE), Jonah (SE), Priya (DevAdv) - Redwood; Liam (CTO), Sara (Lead ML), Diego (Backend), Nadia (Security) - Zephyr

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda - we're gonna run through the SDK quickstarts for python and ts, go over auth patterns, env setup, and then leave time for security and dedicated questions. does that look right?
[00:12] Liam: yeh that works. main things for us are how quickly we can get a proof of concept running and what auth options look like for our regulated flows.
[00:20] Jonah: perfect, i'll share my screen and start with the python quickstart. apologies if the small text—let me know if you want me to zoom.
[00:28] Jonah: ok so, pip install redwood-inference-sdk, then set REDWOOD_API_KEY as an env var. example code—import redwood, client = redwood.Client(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY')) and then client.chat.create(...) it supports streaming by passing stream=True and you can consume chunked events.
[00:45] Sara: is that the recommended pattern? we prefer not to bake long-lived api keys into infra.
[00:51] Priya: great question. short-lived keys via our session tokens are recommended for public clients; for server-to-server we do ephemeral keys or mTLS for dedicated. also enterprise customers can use SSO/SCIM for user provisioning plus KMS integration for encrypting model logs.
[01:10] Diego: how do you pass in env config for multiple environments? we have staging and prod and we want the same codebase.
[01:15] Jonah: people usually store config in 12-factor env vars. e.g., set REDWOOD_API_KEY and REDWOOD_ENV=prod or set REDWOOD_URL if using Private. For dedicated or private deploys, the SDK accepts a base_url param so your requests go to the dedicated endpoint.
[01:32] Liam: can you show the typescript flow? our frontend team is TS heavy.
[01:36] Jonah: for TS it's npm install @redwood/inference, then import { RedwoodClient } from '@redwood/inference'; const client = new RedwoodClient({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY }); sample usage for completions: await client.generate({ model: 'redwood-1.4' , prompt: 'summarize...' }) streaming is supported with async iterators.
[01:55] Sara: the model names—are those the hosted defaults? we might want to pin a model for consistency.
[02:01] Priya: yes hosted catalog has curated models; you can pin model_version in config. Dedicated gives you control to pin a specific model build and we expose versioning in the console for rollouts.
[02:12] Diego: what's the typical latency if we call from eu-west region to your hosted endpoints?
[02:16] Jonah: on our hosted API average p50 is ~60-80ms for short prompts in eu regions but it depends on model size and batching. for strict SLOs customers usually choose Dedicated in-region which removes a lot of network variance.
[02:30] Nadia: security question: how do logs / audit trails work? if we send PII, can we disable retention or use customer-managed keys?
[02:37] Priya: yes, we support configurable retention windows, and for Private/Dedicated we support KMS integration so logs are encrypted with your keys. For hosted we offer opt-out/retention policies per contract, and SOC2 docs are available.
[02:52] Nadia: ok we'll need the SOC2 + architecture diagram. also curious about RBAC for the console.
[02:58] Maya: we'll share the security pack after the call. RBAC in the console supports roles for admin, developer, auditor and can be integrated with SAML SSO.
[03:08] Liam: excellent. on auth — you mentioned session tokens. can you run the sequence for ephemeral token creation?
[03:14] Jonah: sure. server creates an ephemeral token via the client.create_session endpoint (server-authenticated with service key), then the client exchanges that token in-browser to open a websocket stream. this keeps long-lived keys off the client. code sample in the quickstart repo shows that flow.
[03:34] Sara: are there SDK examples for retries and backoff? we do lots of high-throughput payment scraping so we need robust retry logic and idempotency keys.
[03:41] Jonah: yes, the sdk has a built-in retry helper and supports idempotency_key in request metadata. we recommend exponential backoff with jitter and we'll share a snippet.
[03:52] Diego: what about batching? can the SDK batch multiple requests into a single call?
[03:56] Priya: batching is mostly server-side in Redwood's runtime; you can use our batch endpoints for embeddings or use request bundling helpers in the sdk to group prompt sets. also automatic prefix/KV cache helps if you have repeated contexts.
[04:13] Liam: demo a quick typescript streaming example?
[04:16] Jonah: yep — starting streaming code... (typing sounds) const stream = await client.stream.generate({ model: 'rwd-embed-1', prompt: 'Hello' }); for await (const chunk of stream) { console.log(chunk.text) } you'll handle partial tokens.
[04:33] Sara: lovely. one of our constraints: we want to host inference in our VPC. what's the deployment path?
[04:38] Priya: Private includes a customer-managed control plane option + on-prem package. generally steps: sizing -> network peering/VPC setup -> infra deploy -> model onboarding. for POC we can do a lightweight private trial that runs in a sandbox VPC.
[04:56] Nadia: for KMS, do you support AWS KMS & HSM?
[04:59] Priya: yes AWS KMS and HSM integrations are supported; you can bring-your-own keys for Dedicated and Private.
[05:06] Liam: any blockers we should expect integrating the python sdk into our existing microservices?
[05:10] Jonah: usually none — language bindings are lightweight. the main work is auth and networking. If you're behind strict egress rules, you'll either need a NAT for hosted or go Private. We also have a sidecar pattern if you want to keep tokens off services.
[05:26] Diego: how does the SDK surface model quality monitoring? can we hook evals?
[05:31] Priya: Redwood Optimize includes quality monitoring and you can push prompt/eval sets via API; alerts trigger regressions. we'll share the console screenshots.
[05:41] Maya: quick recap — Jonah will post the python & ts quickstarts and streaming/retry examples; I'll send pricing and Dedicated sizing; Priya will include SOC2 and KMS docs. any other immediate asks?
[05:53] Liam: can we run a simple POC with a 2-week timebox to test latency and cost?
[05:58] Maya: absolutely, we'll propose dates in the follow-up.
[06:02] Sara: one last question — client-side SDK licensing/usage limits?
[06:06] Maya: SDKs are open and provided under our standard developer license; usage and rate limits are enforced at the account level; we'll include quota guidance in the follow-up doc.
[06:15] Nadia: thanks — appreciate the security detail.
[06:18] Jonah: thanks all, i'll drop the repo link in the follow-up chat and include code snippets.
[06:23] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the items discussed.

Notes: transcription has minor errors, occasional speaker overlap labeled correctly most of the time. Shared artifacts: quickstart repo link (to be shared), Dedicated sizing worksheet (to be shared), Redwood SOC2 pack (to be shared).

End of transcript.
